drills.title: Design evaluation and release gates for a support agent
drills.prompt: Design the evaluation and release process for a customer-support agent. It handles 200,000 conversations a month and ships a prompt change every week. The golden set has 400 cases across four task types, and a model judge costs $0.01 per graded case. Human review costs $2 per conversation. Cost is currently $0.02 per conversation, and 12 per cent of conversations escalate to a human. Define the pyramid, the golden set, the judge, the trace data you need, and the gates from offline eval to full rollout.

rubric.criterion: Requirements are stated as numbers before any architecture is chosen.
levels: No numbers; requirements are adjectives such as accurate, safe or cheap.
Some numbers are given, but key ones are missing, such as daily volume or the judging cost per run.
Volume, cost and escalation numbers are stated, but derived figures such as canary sample size or review cost are missing or wrong.
Volume, cost and escalation numbers are stated, and daily volume, canary sample size, judging cost and review cost are derived correctly.

rubric.criterion: The architecture is chosen with an explicit decision rule tied to the numbers.
levels: Evaluation is a single manual review before release, or no stages are named.
Pyramid layers or release stages are listed, but without cadences or gating rules.
Layers have cadences and stages are ordered, but the judge calibration, held-out split or significance rule is left unspecified.
Layers, golden set, judge and four gated stages are specified, each tied to a stated number such as agreement, sample size or a rollback threshold.

rubric.criterion: A trade-off is named and accepted explicitly, with its cost quantified.
levels: No trade-off is mentioned; the design is presented as having no downside.
A trade-off is mentioned in general terms, without saying what is given up.
A specific trade-off is named and accepted, but its cost is not quantified.
A specific trade-off is named, accepted and quantified, and the rejected alternative is stated.

rubric.criterion: A measurement is named that would show the choice was wrong.
levels: No measurement or success signal is given.
A vague signal is given, such as watching quality, with no metric or threshold.
A specific metric is named, but without a threshold or the time window that would trigger a rethink.
A specific metric, threshold and window are named, together with the decision that would change.

outline: Derive the load: 200,000 conversations a month is about 6,700 a day. A 5 per cent canary over three days sees about 1,000 conversations, enough to flag a 3-point rise in the 12 per cent escalation rate.
Derive the eval costs: judging all 400 cases costs $4 a run, so the judge can score every candidate. A human sample of 50 conversations costs $100 a release, or about $400 a month.

Pyramid: schema, tool-contract and loop-bound checks on every commit; about 120 replayed scenarios checking tool order and step counts on every merge; the judged golden set and human sample before each release.
Golden set: 100 cases per task type across three difficulty levels, 100 cases held out from tuning, every incident added as a regression case, and the set versioned with its rubric.
Judge: rubric-bound, evidence-citing and structured, with a separate prompt and model family from the agent, accepted only at 90 per cent within-one accuracy on 200 human-labelled cases.

Gates and traces: offline eval, a day of shadow, a three-day 5 per cent canary, then full rollout. Safety failures block outright, quality blocks only on a significant sign-test loss, and traces carry cost and rung per run.

Trade-off and measurement: accept about four days from merge to full rollout for safer weekly releases. Roll back automatically if escalation rises 3 points or cost exceeds $0.03 per conversation over a day.
